systems.title: 3D Printer
systems.subtitle: Building a vase one layer at a time
systems.summary: An open-frame FDM printer melts plastic filament and draws a twisting vase one thin layer at a time — and the flow physics decides how fast it can go.
overview: A fused-filament (FDM) printer is a hot-glue gun on a robot. A motor pushes a 1.75 mm plastic filament into a heated nozzle, which melts it and squeezes out a line less than half a millimetre wide. Three motors steer the nozzle so the line traces the outline of one slice of the object.

This printer is a bed-slinger: the heated bed slides front to back (Y), the print head slides left to right on a gantry (X), and two lead screws lift the whole gantry by one layer height (Z) when a slice is finished. Watch the bed and the head move together: their combined motion draws the curved, six-lobed wall of the vase.

Speed has a hard limit. The hotend can only melt so much plastic each second, its volumetric flow. Faster moves or thicker layers ask for more; past the limit the plastic leaves the nozzle half-melted and the layers do not bond. The settings below compute flow, filament use and print time for the whole vase.

controls.label: Print speed
controls.help: How fast the nozzle moves along the wall.

controls.label: Layer height
controls.help: Thinner layers look smoother but take longer.

controls.label: Nozzle temperature
controls.help: Each plastic has its own melting window.

steps.title: Slicing
body: Before printing, software called a slicer cuts the 3D model into hundreds of thin horizontal slices and writes each outline as G-code: a list of moves such as G1 X12.3 Y4.5 E0.08, meaning move here while pushing out this much filament.
This vase at 0.2 mm layers becomes 320 slices; the controller on the front reads them one line at a time.

steps.title: Heating up
body: The bed heats first, to 60 °C for PLA, so the first layer stays soft enough to grip the textured sheet instead of curling up as it cools.

The nozzle then heats to its window: PLA prints at about 190–220 °C, PETG at 225–250 °C. A thermistor in the heater block measures the temperature many times a second and the controller adjusts the power to hold it steady.

steps.title: The first layer
body: The first layer is pressed slightly into the bed so it spreads and sticks. Four orange knobs under the bed level it to within a few hundredths of a millimetre — paper thickness matters here.
A badly levelled bed is the most common cause of a failed print.

steps.title: Drawing a wall
body: For each layer the nozzle traces the outline twice to make a wall two lines thick. Because this printer moves the bed in Y and the head in X, every curve is the sum of two straight motions, coordinated by stepper motors that move in steps of a few micrometres.
The fan on the head blows on the fresh plastic so it sets quickly and keeps its shape.

steps.title: Layer change
body: When the outline closes, both lead screws turn together and lift the gantry by exactly one layer height. The next layer is laid on top of the still-warm one below and fuses to it.
The vase twists because each slice is rotated a little from the last, and it bulges where the outline grows wider.

steps.title: Flow limits
body: Volumetric flow is speed × layer height × line width. A standard hotend melts about 15 mm³ of PLA per second; flexible TPU only about 4, because it buckles if pushed hard.
Try raising the speed and the layer height together until the flow gauge turns red: beyond that, the printer would lay down cold, weak, under-filled lines.

parts.name: Print head
parts.role: Carries the extruder motor, the part-cooling fan and the hotend that melts the filament.

parts.name: X gantry
parts.role: Two steel rods and a belt that carry the print head left and right.

parts.name: Heated bed
parts.role: A heated aluminium plate under a textured sheet; it slides front to back on rods.

parts.name: Printed vase
parts.role: The part being built, two lines thick, one 0.1–0.36 mm layer at a time.

parts.name: Filament
parts.role: A 1.75 mm plastic strand pulled from the spool into the extruder.

parts.name: Filament spool
parts.role: Usually holds 1 kg of filament, about 330 m of PLA.

parts.name: Spool holder
parts.role: Lets the spool turn freely as filament is pulled off.

parts.name: Z lead screws
parts.role: Brass-nut screws that lift the gantry exactly one layer at a time.

parts.name: Z motors
parts.role: Two stepper motors that turn the lead screws in sync.

parts.name: Z linear rods
parts.role: Guide the gantry so it rises perfectly straight.

parts.name: Z frame
parts.role: The upright aluminium extrusions that hold the gantry.

parts.name: Base frame
parts.role: Aluminium extrusions with T-slots that hold everything square.

parts.name: Y linear rods
parts.role: Hardened steel rods the bed slides on.

parts.name: Y motor
parts.role: Pulls the bed back and forth with a toothed belt.

parts.name: Power supply
parts.role: Converts mains power to 24 volts for the heaters and motors.

parts.name: Controller & display
parts.role: Reads the G-code and drives every motor and heater; the screen shows layer and temperatures.

systems.accuracy: Flow, filament length, mass and time are computed from the vase geometry with two 0.45 mm walls and a solid base; real slicers add acceleration limits, travel moves and cooling pauses, so actual times are longer.
sources: Prusa Research knowledge base: material guides and volumetric flow
Gibson, Rosen & Stucker, Additive Manufacturing Technologies, 3rd ed. (2021)

systems.title: Chocolate Factory
systems.subtitle: From cocoa bean to wrapped bar
systems.summary: A complete bean-to-bar line: roast, winnow, grind, conche, temper, deposit, cool and wrap — and why chocolate must be tempered to snap.
overview: A chocolate bar starts as the bitter seed of a tropical fruit. Fermented and dried on the farm, cocoa beans arrive at the factory hard and sour. Eight machines, working one after another, turn them into the glossy bar that snaps cleanly and melts on your tongue.

Heat does most of the work. The roaster develops flavour; the melanger's granite rollers grind nibs so fine — under 20 micrometres — that the tongue cannot feel the particles; the conche stirs warm chocolate for hours to drive off sharp acids and coat every grain of sugar in cocoa butter.

The cleverest step is tempering. Cocoa butter can crystallise in six different forms, and only Form V gives gloss and snap. The tempering machine melts every crystal, cools the chocolate to seed new ones, then warms it just enough to melt all but Form V. Slide the working temperature and watch what goes wrong when it is out of the window.

controls.label: Working temperature
controls.help: The temperature the chocolate is held at after seeding. Keep it inside the Form V window.

controls.label: Roast temperature
controls.help: Hotter roasts darken the beans and push flavour from fruity to roasty.

controls.label: Line speed
controls.help: Each mould holds four 100 g bars.

steps.title: Roasting
body: Fermented beans tumble in a gas-heated drum at 110–150 °C for 15 to 40 minutes. Sugars and amino acids react (the Maillard reaction), creating hundreds of flavour compounds and the familiar chocolate aroma.
A rotating sieve in front cools the batch quickly so the roast stops exactly where the roaster wants it. Try the roast slider: the sight glass and the cooled beans darken as the temperature rises.

steps.title: Cracking & winnowing
body: The roasted beans are cracked into pieces called nibs. A stream of air from the blower lifts away the light, papery shells, while the heavier nibs fall through.
A cyclone on top spins the air so the shells drop out into the bin — they become garden mulch or animal feed — and the clean nibs travel on to the grinder.

steps.title: Grinding
body: In the melanger two granite rollers roll round a granite bed. Nibs are about half fat (cocoa butter), so as they are crushed they melt into a thick, dark liquid called cocoa liquor.
Sugar and, for milk chocolate, milk powder are added from the hoppers above. Grinding continues until particles are below about 20 micrometres — smaller than the tongue can detect.

steps.title: Conching
body: The conche stirs and kneads the warm chocolate, 10 to 18 hours depending on the recipe. Aeration drives off volatile acids and water, and friction coats every particle in cocoa butter.
The result is smoother, mellower and more liquid. The name comes from the shell shape of the first trough, invented by Rodolphe Lindt in 1879.

steps.title: Tempering
body: Cocoa butter can set in six crystal forms. Only Form V is glossy, snaps cleanly and melts just below body temperature. The tempering machine first melts all crystals at 45–50 °C, then cools the chocolate to seed new ones, then warms it to the working temperature, which melts every form except V.

Each chocolate has its own window: about 31–32 °C for dark, 29–30 °C for milk and 28–29 °C for white, because milk fat interferes with the crystals. Too warm and the seeds melt: the bars bloom grey and soft. Too cool and unstable crystals thicken the chocolate.

steps.title: Depositing
body: A piston depositor fills every cavity of each mould with an exact dose, here 100 g per bar, four bars per mould. The moulds are polished polycarbonate, so each bar takes a mirror shine from them.
The moulds are shaken as they move on, which brings air bubbles to the surface so the bars have no holes.

steps.title: Cooling
body: The filled moulds ride through a tunnel chilled to about 12 °C. As Form V crystals grow, the chocolate contracts slightly, which is what lets the bars drop out of the moulds.
Cooling too fast or too cold causes condensation and sugar bloom, so the tunnel controls temperature and humidity along its length.

steps.title: Wrapping
body: Moulds are turned over and tapped; the bars fall out and the empty moulds return under the line. A flow wrapper folds gold foil and a paper sleeve around each bar.
The wrapped bars are counted into cartons. Store them at 15–18 °C: warmer, and cocoa butter migrates to the surface as fat bloom.

systems.title: Four-Stroke Engine
systems.subtitle: How a spark turns fuel into rotation
systems.summary: A sectioned air-cooled single: watch the crank, rod and piston trade straight-line force for rotation while two cams open the valves in time with the spark.
overview: Almost every car, motorcycle, lawn mower and generator on Earth runs on the same idea, patented by Nikolaus Otto in 1876: draw in a charge of air and fuel, squeeze it, set it alight, and let the hot gas push a piston. Because each of those jobs needs its own trip of the piston, the cycle takes four strokes and two full turns of the crankshaft.

This teaching engine is cut in half so you can see every part move together. The slider-crank turns the piston's up-and-down motion into rotation. A toothed belt drives two camshafts at exactly half crank speed, so each valve opens once every two turns. The plug fires a few degrees before top dead centre, timed so that peak pressure arrives just after it, when the crank can use it.

Every number on the screen comes from one model: the true slider-crank geometry, sin² valve lift windows, a polytropic compression, a Wiebe burn curve and an exhaust blowdown. The indicator diagram traces the pressure against volume, and the area inside its loop is the work done each cycle.

controls.label: Engine speed
controls.help: The animation is slowed so you can follow it; the ×-gauge says by how much.

controls.label: Throttle
controls.help: Opens the intake: more air in, a bigger charge, a higher peak pressure.

steps.title: Intake
body: The piston falls from top dead centre while the cam on the left presses its bucket down and opens the intake valve. The falling piston lowers the pressure in the cylinder, and the atmosphere pushes a fresh charge of air and fuel in through the port.
The valve opened 10° before the piston reached the top and stays open 40° past the bottom, so the moving air keeps filling the cylinder by its own momentum.

steps.title: Compression
body: Both valves are shut. The piston rises and squeezes the 447 cc charge into the 45 cc chamber, a compression ratio of 10 to 1. The gas heats as it is compressed, and its pressure climbs from below one bar to about twenty.
Compressing first is what makes the engine efficient: the hotter and denser the charge when it burns, the more of its heat becomes work.

steps.title: Ignition
body: A few degrees before top dead centre the plug sparks. The flame does not explode at once; it spreads out from the electrode as a front, burning the charge over about fifty degrees of crank rotation.

Firing early gives the flame a head start, so peak pressure lands roughly 15° after the top, where the connecting rod has leverage on the crank. At high speed the spark has to come earlier still, so the gauge of spark advance rises with rpm.

steps.title: Power
body: The burning gas reaches its peak pressure, around 45 bar at full throttle, and drives the piston down. This is the only stroke that makes work; the heavy crank web and counterweight store some of it as momentum to carry the engine through the other three.
Watch the indicator diagram: the curve now runs far above the compression line, and the area between them is the energy delivered to the crank.

steps.title: Exhaust
body: Forty degrees before the bottom the right-hand cam opens the exhaust valve. The still-pressurised gas rushes out on its own, in a blowdown, and the rising piston then sweeps the rest out through the port to the silencer.
For a moment near the top both valves are slightly open together. This overlap lets the outgoing exhaust help draw in the next charge, and the cycle starts again.

parts.name: Piston
parts.role: A light aluminium plug sealed by three rings. Gas pressure on its crown is the only force that drives the engine.

parts.name: Connecting rod
parts.role: A forged I-section link. Its big end is clamped round the crankpin by a cap and two bolts; the small end rides on the piston pin.

parts.name: Crankshaft
parts.role: An overhung crankpin on a web with a drilled counterweight. Its 40 mm throw gives the 80 mm stroke.

parts.name: Intake camshaft
parts.role: Blue lobe. Turns at half crank speed and presses the intake bucket down for 230° of the cycle.

parts.name: Exhaust camshaft
parts.role: Orange lobe. Opens the exhaust valve 40° before bottom dead centre and closes it 10° after the top.

parts.name: Intake valve
parts.role: A steel poppet valve held shut by a green coil spring. Opens up to 8 mm to let the charge in.

parts.name: Exhaust valve
parts.role: Made of heat-resistant steel that turns straw and blue in service: it runs at around 700 °C.

parts.name: Spark plug
parts.role: A ceramic-insulated electrode that fires a spark of about 20,000 volts across a gap of under a millimetre.

parts.name: Cylinder barrel
parts.role: A black cast-iron barrel with thin cooling fins that shed combustion heat into the passing air.

parts.name: Cylinder head
parts.role: Cast aluminium. Holds the valves, the ports (blue for intake, orange for exhaust) and the combustion chamber roof.

parts.name: Head studs
parts.role: Four long studs clamp head, gasket and barrel to the crankcase against 45 bar of pressure.

parts.name: Crankcase
parts.role: Carries the main bearing and the oil. The section faces painted red show where the model was cut.

parts.name: Engine oil
parts.role: Splashed by the crank, it lubricates the bearings and cylinder wall and carries heat away.

parts.name: Dipstick
parts.role: Pull it out to check the oil level between its two marks.

parts.name: Timing belt
parts.role: A toothed rubber belt: 14 teeth on the crank, 28 on each cam, so the cams turn exactly once every two crank turns.

parts.name: Air filter
parts.role: A pleated paper element that stops dust from scouring the cylinder.

parts.name: Throttle body
parts.role: A butterfly valve that sets how much air the engine can breathe, and so its power.

parts.name: Intake runner
parts.role: Carries the air from the throttle to the port. Its length is tuned so pressure waves help fill the cylinder.

parts.name: Fuel injector
parts.role: Fed by the blue line from the yellow fuel pump on the bench, it sprays a metered mist of petrol into the port just before the intake valve opens.

parts.name: Exhaust header
parts.role: Carries the hot exhaust away; its steel turns blue from the heat.

parts.name: Silencer
parts.role: Chambers and perforated tubes inside break up the pressure pulses that would otherwise be a loud bang.

parts.name: Ignition coil
parts.role: A transformer that turns 12 volts into a short pulse of about 20,000 volts for the spark plug.

parts.name: Cam cover
parts.role: Unbolted and set down on the bench so you can see the cams. Its fins baffle the oil mist inside.

parts.name: Tachometer
parts.role: Reads engine speed in thousands of rpm; the red zone starts at 6,000.

parts.name: Pressure gauge
parts.role: Fed by the copper line from a transducer in the head, it follows the pressure inside the cylinder in real time.

parts.name: Test console
parts.role: The bench instrument box that holds the tachometer and the cylinder-pressure gauge.

facts.label: Valve timing
facts.value: IVO 10° BTDC · IVC 40° ABDC · EVO 40° BBDC · EVC 10° ATDC

systems.accuracy: Kinematics are exact for the given geometry. Cylinder pressure uses a single-zone model (polytropic n = 1.32, Wiebe burn, exponential blowdown) that reproduces typical spark-ignition values; real engines differ with port design, mixture and heat loss.
sources: Heywood, Internal Combustion Engine Fundamentals, 2nd ed. (2018)
Pulkrabek, Engineering Fundamentals of the Internal Combustion Engine (2004)

systems.title: Human Heart
systems.subtitle: Four chambers, four valves, one beat
systems.summary: A sectioned heart beats through the cardiac cycle: chambers squeeze, valves snap shut, blood flows, and an ECG traces the electricity that times it all.
overview: Your heart is two pumps side by side. The right side receives tired, oxygen-poor blood from the body and pushes it through the lungs. The left side receives fresh blood from the lungs and drives it out to every cell, around 100,000 times a day.

Each side has two chambers. A thin-walled atrium collects blood; a thick, muscular ventricle pumps it out. Four one-way valves keep the flow moving forward: the tricuspid and mitral valves between atria and ventricles, the pulmonary and aortic valves at the exits. Their closing makes the familiar lub-dub of the heartbeat.

This model is cut along the heart's long axis so all four chambers show at once. Everything moves to the same clock: the cardiac cycle traced by Carl Wiggers in 1915. Switch to Electrical to watch the impulse leave the sinoatrial node, pause at the AV node and race down the ventricles — the same wave the ECG records.

controls.label: Heart rate
controls.help: Resting adults run 60–100 bpm; hard exercise can exceed 170.

controls.label: Slow motion
controls.help: Stretch each beat so you can follow the valves.

steps.title: Two pumps
body: Blue blood returning from the body enters the right atrium through the superior and inferior venae cavae. Red blood from the lungs enters the left atrium through four pulmonary veins.
The thick wall between the two sides, the septum, keeps the oxygen-poor and oxygen-rich blood from ever mixing.

steps.title: Atrial kick
body: The beat begins at the sinoatrial node, the heart's natural pacemaker in the right atrium. Its signal makes both atria contract (the P wave on the ECG) and top up the ventricles with a last 15–20 ml.
Most filling has already happened passively; the atrial kick adds about a fifth, and matters most during exercise.

steps.title: Lub: valves close
body: The impulse pauses briefly at the AV node, then races down the ventricles (the QRS spike). The ventricles squeeze, pressure inside jumps above the atria, and the tricuspid and mitral valves slam shut — the first heart sound, lub.
For a moment all four valves are closed and the ventricles tense without changing volume: isovolumic contraction. Thin cords, the chordae tendineae, stop the valve leaflets turning inside out.

steps.title: Ejection
body: When left-ventricular pressure passes the 80 mmHg in the aorta, the aortic valve opens and about 70 ml of blood is thrown out; the right ventricle does the same into the pulmonary artery at a much lower 25 mmHg.
The left ventricle ejects roughly 60 % of what it holds — the ejection fraction doctors measure.

steps.title: Dub: relaxation
body: The ventricles relax (the T wave). Their pressure falls below the arteries, blood starts to flow back and snaps the aortic and pulmonary valves shut — the second sound, dub.
With all valves closed again the muscle relaxes further (isovolumic relaxation) until its pressure drops below the atria.

steps.title: Filling
body: The tricuspid and mitral valves swing open and blood that has pooled in the atria rushes into the ventricles. Then filling slows until the next P wave starts the cycle again.
Raise the heart rate: diastole shortens much more than systole, which is why a very fast heart can fill too little and pump less.

parts.name: Right atrium
parts.role: Collects oxygen-poor blood from the body and holds the sinoatrial node, the natural pacemaker.

parts.name: Right ventricle
parts.role: Pumps blood to the lungs through the pulmonary valve at low pressure (about 25 mmHg).

parts.name: Left atrium
parts.role: Receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs through four pulmonary veins.

parts.name: Left ventricle
parts.role: The strongest chamber, with walls about 1 cm thick. Pumps blood to the whole body at about 120 mmHg.

parts.name: Tricuspid valve
parts.role: Three leaflets between right atrium and ventricle; closes at the start of systole.

parts.name: Mitral valve
parts.role: Two leaflets between left atrium and ventricle, tied down by chordae tendineae.

parts.name: Pulmonary valve
parts.role: Three half-moon cusps at the exit to the lungs.

parts.name: Aortic valve
parts.role: Three half-moon cusps at the exit to the body; its closure is the second heart sound.

parts.name: Heart muscle (myocardium)
parts.role: Muscle cells that contract together because electrical signals pass directly between them.

parts.name: Aorta
parts.role: The body's largest artery. It arches over the heart and sends branches to the head and arms.

parts.name: Pulmonary artery
parts.role: Carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to both lungs.

parts.name: Superior vena cava
parts.role: Returns blood from the head, neck and arms.

parts.name: Inferior vena cava
parts.role: Returns blood from the lower body.

parts.name: Pulmonary veins
parts.role: Bring oxygen-rich blood from the lungs into the left atrium.

parts.name: ECG monitor
parts.role: Records the heart's electrical activity: P wave, QRS complex and T wave.

parts.name: ECG electrodes
parts.role: Pads that pick up the tiny voltages the heart makes, about one millivolt.

parts.name: Display stand
parts.role: A walnut stand with a brass rod holding the model.

systems.accuracy: Timing, pressures and volumes follow textbook Wiggers values for a healthy adult at rest and scale with heart rate in a simplified way. The section is a schematic long-axis view: real chambers are three-dimensional and twist as they contract.
sources: Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed. (2020)
Wiggers, Modern aspects of the circulation in health and disease (1915)

systems.title: Orrery: Sun, Earth & Moon
systems.subtitle: Why we have seasons and moon phases
systems.summary: A brass orrery turns through the year: Earth's fixed tilt makes the seasons, its slightly oval orbit changes its distance, and the Moon's position sets its phase.
overview: An orrery is a clockwork model of the solar system, first built in the early 1700s. Turn its crank and a gear train carries the Earth around the Sun once a year and the Moon around the Earth once a month.

The seasons are not caused by distance. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January. They happen because Earth's axis is tilted 23.44° and keeps pointing the same way in space all year. In June the northern hemisphere leans toward the Sun: the Sun climbs higher and days are long. Six months later it leans away.

The Moon shines only by reflected sunlight, and half of it is always lit. Its phase is how much of that lit half we can see from Earth, which depends on where the Moon is in its 29.5-day trip around us. Move the latitude pin and the date to see daylight hours anywhere on Earth.

controls.label: Your latitude
controls.help: Positive is north of the equator. Jakarta is −6°, London +51°.

steps.title: The tilt
body: Earth spins around an axis tilted 23.44° from the plane of its orbit, and that axis always points toward the same place in space, near the Pole Star.
On 21 June the northern half leans toward the Sun. At 51° north the noon Sun stands 62° high and the day lasts more than 16 hours.

steps.title: Winter solstice
body: Half an orbit later the axis has not moved, but the Sun is now on the other side: the northern hemisphere leans away. The noon Sun at 51° north rises only 15°, and daylight shrinks to under 8 hours.
South of the equator it is summer. The seasons are reversed between hemispheres.

steps.title: Equinoxes
body: Twice a year, around 20 March and 23 September, the tilt points neither toward nor away from the Sun. Day and night are close to 12 hours everywhere on Earth.
At the equator the noon Sun is directly overhead on these days.

steps.title: Closest in January
body: Earth's orbit is a slightly stretched ellipse. It is closest to the Sun, 0.983 AU or 147 million km, around 3 January, and farthest, 1.017 AU, around 4 July.
That 3 % change in distance makes sunlight about 7 % stronger in January — yet it is winter in the north, which shows how much more the tilt matters.

steps.title: Moon phases
body: The Moon circles the Earth every 29.5 days from new moon to new moon. When it lies between Earth and Sun, its lit side faces away: new moon. Opposite the Sun, we see the whole lit face: full moon.
Halfway between are the quarters, when exactly half of the disc we see is lit.

parts.name: Sun
parts.role: The lamp at the centre. Real Sun: 1.39 million km across, 109 times the Earth.

parts.name: Earth

systems.accuracy: Earth's position uses Kepler's equation of the centre, declination and daylight include atmospheric refraction; sizes and distances are not to scale (a true-scale Earth would be a speck). Moon phases are computed for 2026 from the 18 January new moon.

systems.title: Pin-Tumbler Lock
systems.subtitle: Why only the right key turns
systems.summary: Slide a key into a sectioned brass lock and watch five spring-loaded pin stacks rise until every split lands on the shear line.
overview: Most front doors are held by a pin-tumbler lock, an idea patented by Linus Yale Jr. in the 1860s from a design thousands of years old. Inside a fixed brass shell sits a cylinder called the plug, and the key's job is simply to let the plug turn.

Five holes are drilled through the shell into the plug. Each holds a stack: a key pin at the bottom, a driver pin above it and a spring pushing both down. With no key, the driver pins straddle the gap between shell and plug and jam it.

The right key lifts each key pin by exactly its own length, so every gap between key pin and driver pin lands on the shear line at once. Then nothing crosses the gap and the plug can rotate. Try the wrong key: one or two pins line up, but the plug stays locked.

controls.label: Turn the key
controls.help: Only turns when every pin split sits on the shear line.

steps.title: Locked at rest
body: With no key in the lock, the springs push every pin stack down as far as it will go. Each driver pin now sits half in the shell and half in the plug, like a bolt dropped across the gap.
Try to turn the plug and the five driver pins shear-block it: that is why the dashed line between shell and plug is called the shear line.

steps.title: Sliding the key in
body: The key's tip is ramped, so as it slides in it lifts each pin stack up and lets it drop again into the cuts behind. You can feel this as the clicks of a key going in.
The cuts are called the bitting. This key's bitting is 3-7-4-8-2: the deeper the number, the deeper the cut.

steps.title: On the shear line
body: Fully inserted, each cut sits under its pin. Because every key pin was ground to match its cut, each split between key pin and driver pin now lies exactly on the shear line — the green dots.
With no pin crossing the line, the plug is free to turn and its cam at the back draws the bolt.

steps.title: The wrong key
body: A different key lifts some pins too high, pushing a key pin up across the shear line, and leaves others too low, leaving a driver pin across it. One misplaced pin is enough to stop the plug.
With ten depths and five pins there are 100,000 bitting combinations, though manufacturing rules reduce the usable number.

steps.title: Why picking works
body: No lock is perfect: the holes are never exactly in line, so under a light turning force one pin binds first. A lock-picker lifts that pin until it sets at the shear line, then the next, and so on.
Security pins with spool or serrated shapes, and tighter tolerances, make this much harder.

parts.name: Cylinder shell
parts.role: The fixed brass housing, drilled with five pin chambers. Shown cut in half; section faces are hatched.

parts.name: Plug
parts.role: The cylinder that turns when the right key is in. Its keyway accepts only blades of the right profile.

parts.name: Key pin
parts.role: Brass pins of different lengths, each matched to one cut of the right key.

parts.name: Driver pin
parts.role: Equal-length steel pins that block the shear line unless lifted exactly right.

parts.name: Spring
parts.role: Pushes each pin stack down onto the key.

parts.name: Key
parts.role: Its cuts (bitting) lift each pin stack by the right amount.

parts.name: Shear line
parts.role: The boundary between shell and plug. The lock opens only when every pin split lands on it.

parts.name: Face plate
parts.role: The visible front of the lock, with the keyway opening.

parts.name: Display block
parts.role: A walnut block holding the cutaway on two saddles.

systems.accuracy: Pin and cut proportions are enlarged for clarity; real depth steps are around 0.38 mm (0.015 in) and the plug's rotation is shown at its tailpiece.
sources: Tobias, Locks, Safes, and Security, 2nd ed. (2000)
